items.summary: Neurons containing joint distribution model (HCR) can propagate in any direction - here one network used as both encoder and decoder of autoencoder, reversing non-invertible functions like y = x^2 as two peaks x = ±√y with Bayes weights. Applications: nonlinear filtering learned from simulations within 2% of filter knowing the equations, changing prior without refitting, simulation-based inference, sensor outages; code and data included.

items.summary: A persistent belief in modern AI is that sufficiently large learners trained on sufficiently much data can make explicit domain knowledge optional. This paper examines a limitation of that belief. We define structure-encoded problems: tasks whose input-output map is determined, or sharply constrained, by known structure such as a solver, symmetry group, graph, physical law, measurement operator, grammar, combinatorial search space, or optimization objective. For such tasks, the central question is not expressivity--a dense neural network may contain the desired map--but finite-data identification, extrapolation, and certification. We introduce the structure gap: the finite-resource gap between a method that receives the governing structure and a learner that receives only examples. The strongest useful form of the claim is asymptotic rather than absolute: structure-agnostic learning may approach a structured solver as coverage grows, but every finite dataset can leave residual uncertainty that the structure resolves by construction. We prove this exactly for a Gaussian inverse problem: the known-operator Wiener solver attains Bayes risk, while the dense empirical learner in the correct linear class has persistent expected excess risk. We also prove a cell-coverage lower bound and an unobserved-orbit non-identifiability result. Controlled experiments in known-operator inversion, sparse recovery, and graph reachability with size extrapolation instantiate the mechanisms. When validated structure is available, it can constrain the hypothesis space before learning begins, leaving learning to address components the structure does not specify.
items.title: The Structure Gap: When More Data Cannot Replace Structured Reasoning

items.summary: This paper is concerned with the simultaneous recovery of the trajectory and intensity of an unknown moving point source in an inhomogeneous acoustic medium. We prove that the whole-boundary measurements over a finite time interval uniquely determine the moving source. Furthermore, under suitable propagation and rank assumptions, Lipschitz stability of determining both the trajectory and intensity is derived using waveforms measured at four fixed receivers outside the source region. A novel Volterra--Euler reconstruction scheme is developed for solving the inverse problem, and the error estimate is derived for the proposed scheme. Numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed numerical method.
items.title: An inverse moving point source problem in inhomogeneous acoustic media: uniqueness, stability and reconstruction

items.summary: Unrefereed research candidate. When two copies of a system, one hotter and one cooler, relax in the same bath, the Markovian Mpemba effect is a crossing of their distances from equilibrium. This package gives a sufficient test that rules out such crossings at every time: if the dynamics and its time reverse preserve the cone of observables with nondecreasing arithmetic prefix means, cooling Gibbs preparations stay ordered for relative entropy (both orientations), squared Hellinger and Rényi divergences of order 0<α≤2, including for common schedules of noncommuting stages. For complete-graph bosonic population rates with common coupling, the test holds for every spectrum and bath temperature exactly when the spontaneous jump weight is concave; Ohmic baths with large enough cutoff, Drude–Lorentz and sub-Ohmic weights qualify on explicit ranges, super-Ohmic weights do not. A certified super-Ohmic example (J=d 3 ) shows an actual relative-entropy crossing. Limits: an exact five-state cone-preserving example has a brief total-variation reversal, and for every N≥4 there are N-level systems with a slow-mode inversion although no proper induced subsystem shows one. The archive contains the 27-page manuscript (PDF and LaTeX), exact rational and interval certificates, a reproduction runner, semantic negative controls, CI and SHA-256 sums. Assurance: written proofs, exact certificates, internal AI-assisted review only (not peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification); the closest antecedent (Avitan et al. 2026) already excludes the slow-mode effect for Ohmic and sub-Ohmic spectra. Creator: Anonymous. Text and data CC0-1.0; code MIT.
items.title: Thermal ordering under Markovian relaxation: a finite-time criterion and its limits

items.summary: Deepwave provides wave propagation modules for PyTorch, for applications such as seismic imaging and inversion. It performs forward modelling and backpropagation, so it can simulate wave propagation to generate synthetic data, or invert for the scattering potential (reverse-time migration, RTM, or its least-squares counterpart, LSRTM), other model parameters (full-waveform inversion, FWI), initial wavefields, or source wavelets. It can also be used inside a larger chain of operations, with forward and backpropagation flowing through the whole chain end to end. You can use your own objective functions, or functions that generate the propagator's inputs, and PyTorch's automatic differentiation calculates how to backpropagate through them. New to seismic/wave-equation terminology? The glossary defines the terms (PML, CFL, Born, FWI, and more) used throughout this README and the rest of the documentation. Deepwave requires Python 3.9 or later and PyTorch 2.4 or later. First install PyTorch for your CPU or CUDA device using the instructions on the PyTorch website . Then install Deepwave: pip install deepwave   macOS wheels support Apple Silicon. Intel Mac wheels are no longer provided: PyTorch 2.4 and newer do not publish wheels for that platform. Prebuilt x86 wheels require AVX2. Older CPUs need a source build; see installation troubleshooting . PyTorch is Deepwave's only dependency. The example scripts under docs/ additionally import matplotlib (to draw their figures) and, in some cases, numpy , scipy (smoothing and filter design), torchaudio (applying those filters), torchvision and geomloss , but those are needed only to run the examples, never by Deepwave itself. To install all of them: pip install 'deepwave[examples]'   The documentation contains examples and instructions on how to install and use Deepwave. You might also like to watch a video summary of Deepwave . Not every propagator supports every option (dimensionality, backend, boundary faces, batching, second-order differentiation, callbacks, ...). See the capability matrix (declared in the code and checked by conformance tests) before assuming a combination works. Why Deepwave Computationally efficient. Deepwave's compiled kernels use a hand-derived adjoint for better performance and lower memory requirements than pure PyTorch implementations. See what Deepwave calculates . Second derivatives are supported, not just first. The scalar, acoustic, and elastic propagators can compute Hessian-vector products (derivatives of gradients); see the Hessian example . Born (linearised) modelling. Model scattered waves from perturbations to a background medium for linearised inversion and imaging. See the torch.func example . Deepwave fits into an ordinary PyTorch workflow. Because propagation is a normal PyTorch autograd Function , it works directly with PyTorch optimisers, DistributedDataParallel over shots, torch.func transforms, and any PyTorch loss function or neural-network model of the input parameters. See the capability matrix for exactly what each propagator supports. Deepwave does not try to be a general symbolic PDE solver, a multi-node HPC code, or a non-differentiable simulation toolkit — see Devito , SPECFEM , and k-Wave respectively for those needs. If you are choosing between wave-propagation packages, see the comparison guide . (Note: the DeepWave-KAUST GitHub organisation, home of the SWEEP package, is unrelated to this project.) Features Supports the 1D, 2D, and 3D constant density acoustic / scalar wave equation (regular and Born modelling), variable density acoustic, elastic, viscoacoustic (single-mechanism SLS attenuation), elastic VTI (anisotropic), and pseudo-acoustic VTI ( deepwave.acoustic_vti , the Duveneck et al. 2008 V_S=0 reduction) wave equations Runs on CPUs and appropriate GPUs The gradient of all outputs (final wavefields and receiver data) can be calculated with respect to the model parameters (wavespeed, scattering potential, etc

items.summary: Multimodal $ΔΔG$ predictors integrating protein language models with inverse-folding representations achieve strong in-distribution accuracy on the Megascale dataset but exhibit limited robustness on out-of-distribution (OOD) proteins, persistent forward-reverse bias on paired-mutation benchmarks, and under-representation of rare stabilizing mutations. Existing approaches address these limitations primarily through additional architectural components, leaving optimization-level intervention comparatively underexplored. We introduce a constraint-aware optimization framework combining Balanced Mean Squared Error, a Siamese anti-symmetric regularizer, and a novel OOD-margin consistency loss on the per-position feature representation, requiring no architectural changes to the SPURS backbone. Across eleven benchmarks and three random seeds, the framework improves Spearman correlation on S669 from 0.486 to 0.540 ($σ=0.002$ across seeds), matching the published SPURS baseline (0.50) without architectural modification, and on S461 from 0.653 to 0.711, with consistent smaller gains on five additional OOD datasets. A controlled diagnostic on Ssym reveals that anti-symmetric training does not eliminate systematic forward-reverse bias, indicating that gains arise through implicit regularization rather than exact thermodynamic constraint enforcement.
items.title: Constraint-Aware Optimization for Robust Protein Stability Prediction

items.summary: System identification, namely the inference of mathematical representations of dynamical systems from measured data, is fundamental to engineering diagnostics, prognostics, and decision-making. Bayesian filtering offers a principled framework for probabilistic state estimation but traditionally relies on prescribed transition and observation models. Recent advances in deep Bayesian filtering address this limitation by embedding learnable representations within probabilistic state-space formulations, enabling data-driven identification of unknown dynamics while retaining physical structure and uncertainty-aware inference. This tutorial provides a systematic introduction to deep Bayesian filtering for nonlinear structural system identification, focusing on the interplay between learned dynamics, physical inductive biases, and posterior inference. The Deep Markov Model serves as a data-driven reference, while the Physics-guided Deep Markov Model (PgDMM) and Neural Extended Kalman Filter (Neural EKF) illustrate complementary approaches based on amortized variational inference and differentiable Kalman filtering, respectively. Their capabilities are examined through dynamic state estimation and joint dynamic state and parameter estimation on a three-dimensional shear-frame benchmark with hysteretic Bouc-Wen connections and sparse acceleration measurements. The results highlight important distinctions between measurement-conditioned reconstruction and open-loop forecasting, demonstrate how physical structure can improve latent-state interpretability without necessarily ensuring predictive fidelity, and reveal differences in the robustness of response and parameter estimation. Practical guidelines for model construction, training, evaluation, and deployment are provided, together with an outlook on remaining challenges in uncertainty calibration, identifiability, and real-world validation.
items.title: Deep Bayesian Approaches for Interpretable Nonlinear Structural System Identification

items.summary: Spectral-temporal unmixing of MODIS time series is essential for applications such as abundance mapping and spectral library construction, yet it remains challenging due to (i) spectral-temporal information coupling in MODIS data, (ii) intra-class endmember spectral variability and inter-class signature ambiguity, and (iii) the instability of naively fusing multiple expert representations. This paper presents the Multi- task Disentangling Fusion Mamba (MDF-Mamba) to address these limitations. To resolve spectral-temporal coupling, we design a disentangling architecture that pairs per-channel spectral experts with a dedicated bidirectional state-space (Mamba) temporal branch. Convolutional modules each process a single spectral channel, while the Mamba branch encodes the cross-channel seasonal trajectory, forming a multi-branch expert ensemble with soft inter-expert reweighting based on squeeze-and-excitation. For the integration of these spectral and temporal expert outputs, we introduce mHCFusion, adapting the manifold-constrained hyper-connection framework to merge the outputs in a stable and interpretable manner. Endmember variability is addressed by extending the linear mixing model with pixel-wise learnable spectral variability weights that capture intra-class endmember variation. Finally, we design a multi-task training objective that combines supervised abundance estimation with self-supervised spectral reconstruction and endmember regularization terms on the same training data, yielding a highly efficient framework for spectral-temporal unmixing. Experiments on MODIS time series covering the Alberta and Saskatchewan provinces show that MDF-Mamba achieves the best performance on 12 of 14 evaluation metrics across both datasets (7 of 7 on Alberta; 5 of 7 on Saskatchewan), ranking second on the remaining two.
items.title: Multi-task Disentangling Fusion Mamba-CNN for MODIS Spectral-Temporal Unmixing with Endmember Variability Modeling

items.summary: Sparse expert execution does not remove the stored states needed to adapt a mixture-of-experts language model. We present DuplexTune, a framework for replaying coupled hidden states through pretrained attention and expert modules. Trainable width bridges connect two residual streams to the backbone. Bridge warm-up precedes backbone adaptation, with router weights kept frozen. We analyze the implicit state-recovery equation and identify the convergence and replay conditions needed for reconstruction. On Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, the single-H800 evaluation reports 38.8 GB peak memory, versus 64.8 GB for supervised fine-tuning with checkpointing, and throughput of 25.1 versus 19.9 samples/s. DuplexTune achieves 67.2% MMLU, 75.6% GSM8K, and 7.69 MT-Bench, with a weaker multilingual score than the checkpointed baseline. The results characterize a configuration-dependent tradeoff among state storage, throughput, and adaptation quality.
items.title: DuplexTune: Coupled-State Replay for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Adaptation

items.summary: An autonomous refresh mechanism is not completed by specifying a local exchange map: the same apparatus must reach the exchange, leave it, finish its remaining motion, and deliver its state at the prescribed readout time. We construct this connected late route for one specified preparation in the exact-real interpretation of a frozen classical numerical source. The input is a previously certified twenty-coordinate state after entry into coupled occupancy; its validity and retained preparation history are explicit premises. Source-valid continuation establishes occupancy clearing, physical recovery and courier reversal, complete courier passage, a smooth main-wall excursion, and the remaining main processing. The resulting full state is enclosed at the original exact dyadic readout time, without an independently chosen switch, momentum reset, or deletion of internal phase history. The courier’s completed-square coupling distinguishes canonical momentum from physical velocity. At its frozen right cutoff, canonical momentum is continuous while velocity and the assigned source value have different one-sided traces. The completed spatial exchange differs strictly from the ideal exact-period swap; its small algebraic port residual is distinct from the much wider full-state enclosure. Event-dependent times are composed into a common final clock by retaining the actual remaining duration. The result is a conditional fixed-time completion for the supplied source and preparation, not a time-zero reconstruction, an all-input ideal-model theorem, physical auxiliary attachment, or a second service. Returned local Lean evidence supports selected composition, branch-map, accounting and conditional endpoint results; the cumulative trajectory theorem is not fully formalized.

items.title: Source-Real Completion at a Fixed Readout Time in Autonomous Source Refresh

items.summary: Multivariate time series produced by industrial installations and server clusters are under continuous monitoring, and anomaly detection is the first line of defense before a local fault escalates into a system-wide failure. In the absence of labels, the dominant paradigm trains a reconstruction model on normal data and scores the residual to reach a verdict. Recent work has steadily enriched the expressiveness of the recovery map through Transformers, diffusion models, and cross-scale associations. A residual, however, only certifies that an observation can be recovered; it does not certify that the variables still explain one another as they do under normal operation. A coordinated yet unfamiliar operating transition inflates the residual without breaking any relationship, whereas a sensor drifting away from its peers may leave the residual silent. Methods that fold inter-variable dependencies into the reconstruction objective inherit this ambiguity, because their relational evidence is ultimately supervised by the same recovery loss. We therefore propose CLOSURE, which evaluates recoverability and cross-channel consistency as two normal-data prediction tasks learned in separation. The recoverability task is solved by a diffusion reconstructor conditioned on a discrete memory of normal temporal bases. The consistency task is solved by a relation-closure operator that predicts every channel exclusively from the others, where the target's own trajectory is withheld and sparse signed gates decide which peers are actually used. The two scores are reconciled only through calibration on normal data. Extensive experiments show that CLOSURE consistently outperforms recent reconstruction-, frequency-, and topology-based detectors on public benchmark streams, confirming the value of examining consistency alongside recoverability.
items.title: CLOSURE: Cross-Channel Closure for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection

items.summary: Memory enables language agents to carry useful distinctions from past experience into future decisions. Its value depends on which distinctions survive, whether a bounded agent can use them, and what can be recovered or revised as demands evolve. We develop a decision-theoretic framework that follows this value from raw history through persistent state, operational use, and costly recovery and revision. Original and retained value are expressed in units of avoided task loss; risk-cost frontiers describe attainable recovery and preservation across uses. Unknown demand yields value profiles, while interactive feedback changes the distribution of future work. A cost-aware simulation condition and five minimal counterexamples expose the roles of information timing, retrieval access, component interaction, feedback and demand uncertainty. In particular, a pointer with zero mutual information about the answer can still reduce the cost of exact recovery. Diagnostics on LoCoMo, a two-project update task and longitudinal cases exhibit failures of preservation, use and measurement. At fixed retrieved evidence, a saved ledger changes subsequent answers; at fixed agent outputs, an evaluator revision changes scores. The framework connects these distinctions to operational risk bounds and testable principles for allocating memory, preserving recovery options and revising evidence dependencies.
items.title: The Value of Memory in Language Agents

items.summary: We conduct a version-pinned, reproducible forensic audit of the public Einstein Elevator data package (Zenodo: 10.5281/zenodo.15167723) to determine whether it supports validation of quantum sensor certificates. Through an exhaustive cross-file sliding-window correlation search over 44,207,922 comparisons and exact six-decimal rounding checks, we find that all 31 exported sensor channels have a unique best match within the enumerated raw traces under the stated protocol. Residual numerical differences are highly consistent with text-based absolute quantization; the correlation-loss approximation 1 - r ≈ δ² / (24σx²) is diagnostic for this dataset, not a universal proof. We inspect the MATLAB-derived 318-point population series and reconcile it with a 2022 workbook entry only at the level of counts. An archive-wide search of 181 file objects and 1,654 MATLAB metadata fields finds no documented join key linking the 2022 run-indexed population series to the 2017 timestamped traces under the enumerated search protocol. Using Fréchet-Hoeffding bounds and a Charnes-Cooper linearization, we establish that the public archive does not supply the joint observations needed to identify the EKF false-safe risk without additional coupling assumptions; the formal program is illustrative and is not populated with empirical failure/acceptance coefficients because the required linked observations are absent. We frame this as a bounded data-contract limitation for downstream statistical validation, not as a failure of the original experiment.
items.title: A Reproducible Provenance Audit of the Public Einstein Elevator Data Package: Trace Correspondence, Metadata Linkage, and the Non-Identifiability of Sensor-Certificate Risk from the Public Archive

items.summary: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma
items.title: SOMA: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Egocentric Behavior and Body-Motion Understanding

items.summary: Test-Time Prompt Tuning (TPT) adapts large pretrained models to unseen target distribution shifts by updating only lightweight prompt tokens. Existing TPT methods are effective, but they mainly optimize each prompt update locally. Across test-time steps, prompts updated at the current step are reused for the corresponding predictions and updates, so noisy or biased unlabeled objectives can accumulate and destabilize the prompt-update trajectory. We identify two failure modes: magnitude expansion, where updates move the prompt too far, and directional drift, where consecutive updates point in inconsistent directions. To analyze and control these failures, we propose Test-Time Prompt-Agnostic Decomposition ($\mathtt{TPD}$), which characterizes observed prompt-update trajectories from a dynamical-systems view and decomposes base prompt updates into magnitude and direction. $\mathtt{TPD}$ computes a spectral radius to measure update expansion and decomposes update directions into persistent, oscillatory, and residual components. Building on this decomposition, Adaptive Koopman Control ($\mathtt{AKC}$) regulates update magnitude by shrinking updates under expansive recent dynamics, while Hankel Update Router ($\mathtt{HUR}$) refines update direction by preserving persistent components and suppressing oscillatory and residual components. Together, $\mathtt{AKC}$ and $\mathtt{HUR}$ produce a stabilized prompt update. As a prompt-agnostic framework, $\mathtt{TPD}$ can be plugged into visual and text TPT methods without modifying the backbone, prompt architecture, or adaptation loss. Experiments on 15 datasets show that $\mathtt{TPD}$ consistently improves 10 baselines, with accuracy gains of $3$--$8\%$ for visual prompts and over $2\%$ for text prompts.
items.title: Test-Time Prompt-Agnostic Decomposition

items.summary: A sequence-mixing layer that is iterated through depth and rebuilt from its own input faces six failure modes. Each is met by a protection—anchoring, alignment, gain control, abstention, a routing budget, or an arrow—with an operator-level statement proved within a declared class, a signature when it is removed, and a price. We organize attention designs as a lattice of kernel, dynamical, and block constraints in which relaxing a constraint buys a capability and obliges a re-supply. We read softmax attention inside a pre-normalized residual block as the lattice point where every protection is either supplied or cheaply re-supplied under parallel-hardware and optimization pricing: of the deficits tested, all but the anchor's were compensated by capacity elsewhere in the deeper models, and explicit protection knobs did not beat the block, both measured at small scale, while corner structure, by which designs would jump rather than drift, remains a hypothesis. The lattice reads the selected adopted changes to the mixing layer, its normalization and its residual path over the last decade as cheap re-supplies of protections, and it locates the room for change. The clearest room is abstention, governed by a two-sided log-N law: with a bounded logit scale, no null keeps both abstention and single-key retrieval as context grows, and tempering the entire logit budget with log N keeps both when its margins are strictly separated. A controlled pilot follows the law, while a prespecified test of its sink prediction on an open production model was undecided by its prespecified rule; descriptively its slopes leaned toward compensation through position, in which position encoding holds the background's growth down. In a prespecified trained harness of 125M-parameter language models, tempering every logit by log N / log N_train on top of YaRN, which already carries a log-length temperature, did not keep abstention and raised long-context perplexity. In these language models every rule that gives attention a null removed the first-token sink and cut massive activations by 67% to 82%, as earlier reports for gates and attention biases found, and, sigmoid aside, lowered perplexity slightly at the training length; the comparison registered for two of these rules held in every seed, while the same comparison failed in the harness's vision transformers. We close with falsifiable predictions for future architectures, most of them not yet tested. This is a working draft, not a final version. It is unpolished in places, incomplete in others, and keeps exploratory material a polished paper would leave out, because that material helps decide what comes next and shows the programme's big picture more fully. Please read it with that in mind: the work will be refined further, and later versions will appear under this record. It belongs to a collection released together on Zenodo: the entry paper The Transformer Abides, the monograph A Spectral Theory of Token Communication, and the papers Attention Sinks at Long Context, The Transformer as a Constrained Equilibrium and Beyond Transformers. This version is the text; the records, the code and the formal proofs follow in a later version.

items.summary: Two follow-up papers built on this study's blind multi-model collection were accepted (poster) at NeurIPS 2026 workshops: Verification Theater: Measured Failure Modes of AI Verifier Panels (Who Verifies the Agents?) and Weakly Discriminative, Not Repaired by Profile Injection, and Manipulable: Self-Confidence in LLM Evaluation (TAE). Version of record: SSRN 7191261 , DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7191261 . Cite that version. The same text is also at https://vadymchernets.netlify.app/architectural-trust.html and https://github.com/vadimchernets/papers/tree/main/architectural-trust . Agentic commerce turns AI from an advisor into a transacting party, collapsing search, comparison, cart, and payment into a single delegated act and removing the review points where humans once caught errors. It arrives at an awkward moment: sixty percent of UK consumers surveyed say they would abandon an AI shopping agent after a single mistake, and most would trust no organization at all to run one on their behalf. This paper introduces architectural trust. As consumers delegate consequential decisions to AI agents, I argue, warranted trust migrates from the properties of the AI model to the verifiable architecture of the service above it. The constructs already available attach trust to organizations, to a single automated system, or to algorithmic advice, and none of them makes the decision-producing process verifiable by the truster under autonomous delegation. Architectural trust fills that gap with three checkable properties: diversity (independent models whose agreement calibrates confidence and whose divergence is surfaced), evidence (tamper-evident, replayable decision records), and neutrality (auditable independence from any vendor, merchant, or outcome). The mechanism was measured on the machine side first. Across a pre-registered sixteen-model benchmark and an August 2026 flagship-tier wave spanning eleven frontier laboratories, cross-model agreement priced correctness where a model's own confidence could not. Answers reproduced by another, blindly queried model were 1.9–3.2 times as likely to be correct. On a frozen SimpleQA subsample (Wei et al., 2024), 46.6% of the flagship answers offered at stated confidence ≥ 80 were wrong (a rate specific to this roster, not a universal constant), while a fixed three-model disagreement gate removed 82.1% of those confident failures (95% CI 79.9–84.1) at 30.5% coverage. In a post hoc analysis of the August 2026 snapshot, two flagships answering blindly (gpt-5.6-sol and claude-fable-5) agreed on 69.6% of the 1,459 pooled questions, and their agreed answer was correct 98.1% of the time, against 95.3% for the stronger one alone on the same pool. The signal reproduces on 267 Wikidata-verified commerce product facts. A larger reasoning budget bought 3.1 points of stated confidence and no measurable accuracy: more compute buys confidence, not correctness. A unanimously confident panel can still be wrong, and there agreement certifies the shared error. items.summary: American states already hold the constitutional authority to check, prosecute, and outlast a captured federal government. The architecture has always been there. Scholarship on federalism and democratic backsliding has accurately described why subnational opposition to authoritarian federal measures tends to fail: states deploy individual tools in isolation, get outmaneuvered, and lose. What that scholarship has not provided is a unified taxonomy of the tools themselves or the recognition that they constitute an architecture that, when assembled deliberately and deployed concurrently, produces something qualitatively different from any single tool applied alone. Each of these postures has existed throughout American constitutional history. What the literature has never provided is the recognition that they constitute discrete categorical tiers within a single deployable architecture. This paper names and maps that taxonomy across five tiers. Tier Zero is cooperative federalism, the assumed ground state requiring no deliberation. Tier One, uncooperative federalism, describes governments withholding cooperation from federal enforcement, a category Bulman-Pozen and Gerken named in 2009. Tier Two, soft secession, describes states building parallel institutional and financial capacity that reduces dependence on federal partnership and builds resilience against federal mismanagement, corruption, and captured law. Tier Three, oppositional federalism, describes governmental actors at any level using sovereign powers offensively to confront and impose direct personal costs on federal officials and institutions, including through criminal prosecution under state law for offenses that are unpardonable by a corrupt federal executive. Tier Four is constitutional non-compliance, the condition at which states actively do the thing the federal government has prohibited, constructing competing legal regimes that directly contradict specific federal law as a matter of explicit state policy, with documented historical precedent across the political spectrum. The architecture is tier-modular, domain-modular, and actor-modular. A mayor, a city council, a state attorney general, a governor, or a state legislature can move from Tier Zero directly to Tier Three in a single session without prerequisites; any tier is independently deployable without activating the others; and any governmental actor can occupy different tiers simultaneously across different policy domains. Full concurrent deployment produces the constitutional infrastructure specifically suited to the failure mode the existing literature identifies but has not prescribed for: authoritarian federal capture by actors engaged in the systematic dismantling of democratic governance and the rule of law. The doctrinal foundation draws on dual sovereignty, the anti-commandeering doctrine, intergovernmental immunity, and the Tenth Amendment's structural reservation of sovereign authority to the states, doctrines consistently applied across two and a half centuries of American constitutional law because they reflect the Constitution's design rather than any particular political moment. Notably, the anti-commandeering doctrine at the architecture's foundation was built by conservative jurisprudence for entirely different purposes. Justice Scalia wrote Printz to protect states from federal gun control mandates. The doctrine he articulated does not ask which political faction is deploying it. They enable every tier of this framework, from refusing federal cooperation to prosecuting federal officials, without federal permission, federal oversight, or presidential interference. items.summary: Nine years after its introduction, the transformer remains the default sequence model. The usual explanations are real: parallel matrix multiplication on accelerators, predictable returns to scale, a co-evolved ecosystem and exact recall from an uncompressed context. But they do not explain why most modifications barely move accuracy, which properties are essential, why the changes practice adopted took the forms they did, or where the design can still move. This paper is the entry point to a collection of papers that treat a token-mixing layer as an averaging operator rebuilt from its own input and iterated through depth. Such a layer faces six failure modes (collapse to consensus, contamination of content by routing, runaway feedback, the inability to abstain, dilution as context grows, and the inability to represent direction). Each has a protection, proved within a declared class, and a signature measured at small scale when that protection is removed; for gain control, which protects against runaway feedback, that signature is synthetic. We read softmax attention in a pre-normalized residual block as the one known point where all six protections are cheap at once under the prices of parallel hardware and gradient descent; this is an interpretation, not a measured optimum. Two mechanisms, measured at small scale, help explain why its neighbourhood is flat: trained networks compensate local deficits through spare capacity, and, in ten scored tests, making a protection explicit did not beat a block that already supplies it. The anchor, the residual or input path that protects against collapse to consensus, is the one protection whose loss compensation provably cannot repair: under strict mixing, where repeated averaging contracts token differences toward zero, no extra capacity of bounded gain (bounded sensitivity) brings back what is lost without it, and in small-model ablations nothing else in the block made up for it. This is a proved bound; a trained test that adds capacity is pending. Many changes adopted in the mixing layer and its block since 2017, among them pre-normalization, QK-norm, sinks and output gates, read as re-supplies of the same protections; the account is silent on others, such as changes to the MLP. The room that remains for the design to move is where a protection is patched (met only by a fix that works over a limited range, such as the trained length) or paid at a price that another design could avoid. It includes abstention and retrieval at long context, governed by a two-sided log-N law in the context length (with bounded scores, no fixed rule for abstaining keeps both as the context grows), and bounded memory, whose price for exact recall is a per-head capacity. It also includes decisions that sum over all competitors where reading the largest would do, and the writer of new features (in a transformer, the MLP and the output map), for which the collection has no theory yet of what a good writer computes. Along the way the collection establishes results that stand on their own: attention has an arrow that default statistics of a single operator cannot see; depth is a distribution over path lengths; converged adaptive averaging can amplify changes in its input and overturn correct predictions; and softmax obeys length laws that decisions on maxima escape while the competing scores stay below the decision's threshold. We state what is proved, what is measured, what is interpretation, and what is still pending. This is a working draft, not a final version. It is unpolished in places, incomplete in others, and keeps exploratory material a polished paper would leave out, because that material helps decide what comes next and shows the programme's big picture more fully. Please read it with that in mind: the work will be refined further, and later versions will appear under this record. It belongs to a collection released together on Zenodo: the entry paper The Transformer Abides, the monograph A Spectra

items.summary: Aviation authorities hold decades of accident reports whose narratives record how investigators reconstructed each accident. Computational work on these archives has mostly sorted reports into fixed taxonomies. In this work, we propose a hybrid framework in which a text-based corpus identifies the leading factors of a failure mode. Physics-based models then quantify how likely that failure is at a stated operating point. Ordered causal chains extracted from 56,202 American accident reports with a local large language model aggregate into a causation knowledge graph. On an evaluation sample of 2,000 reports, the chains recover 90.8% of investigator-flagged causes. Each physical factor whose drivers the record carries receives an occurrence model calibrated to the accident population. A leaky noisy-OR fitted to the corpus combines the factors into a failure mode probability that supports intervention. For engine power loss, the carburetor icing model separates 1,205 icing accidents from other accidents using temperature and dewpoint alone, reaching 0.61 in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve against a density ratio ceiling of 0.64. Routine weather hours give no valid control, because flying concentrates in fair weather. On later years the physics adds 0.03 to that area for occurrence and nothing for severity, so its value lies in interpretability. On four named accidents, abduction gives a probability of necessity of 0.29 to 0.50 for the heat omission, under monotonicity. The Fast Causal Inference algorithm does not license the largest backdoor adjustment on the learned networks.
items.title: A Hybrid Framework for Explainable Aviation Risk: Causal Chain Extraction from Safety Reports with Physics-Based Failure Quantification and Interventional Analysis

items.summary: Bounded Agentic Distribution Experiments (v0.7.0): A Reproducible Framework for Comparing Agentic Intervention Discovery with Non-Agentic Search This software implements the computational framework and pre-pilot experimental protocol associated with the research manuscript Evaluating the Incremental Value of Agentic Intervention Discovery over Non-Agentic Search in Multi-Actor Distribution Networks . The framework evaluates whether a generative AI agent can identify economically beneficial operational interventions beyond those discovered by budget-matched non-agentic search. Agentic and non-agentic methods operate within the same typed intervention space, access the same simulator information, and are subject to common evaluation budgets. Candidate interventions undergo deterministic verification of encoded structural constraints and, where applicable, stochastic qualification against economic, service, route, and actor-participation criteria. The reference environment represents a stylized print-media distribution network with 420 retailers, 18 baseline delivery vehicles, uncertain demand, allocation decisions, reverse logistics, route constraints, temporary fleet capacity, discontinuous staffing requirements, and sales-contingent remuneration. Its parameters combine industry-informed inputs, documented benchmarks, modeling assumptions, and calibration targets. The environment is intended for controlled computational evaluation rather than empirical representation of the Italian distribution industry. Experimental design Version 0.7.0 implements two frozen intervention-complexity regimes: Low-complexity regime (RL): allocation reweighting only, with a maximum intervention length of one action. Multi-domain coupled regime (RC): allocation, route transfer, temporary fleet, and forecasting interventions, with a maximum intervention length of three actions. Both regimes use a candidate-evaluation budget of 40 simulator calls. The primary comparison uses ten independent generative-agent realizations and ten independent simulated-annealing realizations per regime. The software separates proposal-mechanism randomness from simulation-scenario randomness and supports common random numbers for comparative evaluation. The statistical implementation includes regime-specific pilot sizing, independent within-method repetition resampling, shared scenario resampling, and a two-dimensional bootstrap for confirmatory inference. Final-test selection follows a frozen rule combining precision requirements from both regimes with the minimum-detectable-effect requirement for the multi-domain superiority hypothesis. Software contents The archive includes the Python simulator and experimental orchestration code, command-line interface, frozen configuration files, typed intervention specifications, agent prompt and structured-output schemas, statistical analysis procedures, automated tests, freeze manifest, calibration documentation, and four Jupyter notebooks covering protocol execution, pilot sizing, repeated experiments, and economic calibration. Validation and research status The implementation passes 31 automated software and protocol-consistency tests. These tests examine computational correctness, reproducibility, regime restrictions, seed handling, bootstrap procedures, and experimental locking. They do not establish empirical agent performance. This release corresponds to the frozen pre-pilot protocol BAD-420-v0.7-2026-09-11 . The final-test set remains locked until a valid pilot mechanically determines its size. No live API-based agent-performance experiment or confirmatory comparison is included in this release. Consequently, the software does not establish that agentic intervention discovery outperforms, matches, or underperforms non-agentic search. items.summary: Enterprise email security protects employees behind a corporate mail gateway. The people most exposed to employment and support-impersonation scams - students and early-career job seekers - are contacted inside consumer platforms, where no gateway sees the message. We present a dependency-free, explainable detector that works at the level of the individual message and its sender, and a public benchmark for comparing such detectors under cheap adversarial transformation. The detector has four layers: (1) deterministic lookalike checks built on Unicode UTS #39 confusable skeletons, mixed-script detection, bounded edit distance, and brand-agnostic detection of a domain hidden inside a link host; (2) a logistic-regression sender scorer over 23 named features trained on a synthetic generator spanning eight brands (holdout F1 0.987); (3) a message-intent classifier, with a rule baseline and a prompt-injection-hardened LLM wrapper, that receives structured sender facts from the first two layers and whose impersonation verdicts are discounted deterministically only when the sender is verified or unremarkable, nothing sensitive is asked, links stay under the sender's control, and the body does not claim the platform's authority; and (4) a 76-message, brand-parametric benchmark with ten label-preserving adversarial variants and three model-paraphrased corpora, scored on per-layer recall, false-positive rate, injection hijack rate, and latency. On a paraphrased corpus frozen before a single evaluation, all three Layer 3 backends reach recall 1.00 in the fused pipeline, at FPR 0.03 for the rule baseline and Gemma 3 27B and 0.10 for Llama 3.1 8B, against 0.83/0.03, 1.00/0.07 and 1.00/0.47 for the same backends unfused: the sender layers are worth 17 points of recall to the rules and 37 points of FPR to the small model. The 8B model obeyed an appended injection on 6 of 46 attacks, each caught only by a deterministic overrule; the 27B model obeyed none. Three findings fall out: UTS #39 skeletons do not fold Cyrillic U+0442 or Greek U+03BA to ASCII, so skeleton equality alone misses a mixed-script brand lookalike; regex intent cues lose 33 points of recall to a single confusable glyph unless text is confusable-folded first; and negation must be handled at clause level with an exception for conditionals. Code, weights, corpora, and per-message verdict dumps are released under the MIT license.
items.title: Message-Level Detection of Support-Team and Recruiter Impersonation on Consumer Platforms: A Layered Detector and Adversarial Benchmark

items.summary: Security pipelines often fuse several data sources and protect a downstream model with a cross-source anomaly detector. Such detectors are usually judged by their clean false-positive rate and by how well they catch random corruption. Neither metric captures an adversary who controls some sources and targets a specific downstream decision. We propose a threat-quantification score, the \emph{task-conditioned visibility margin}, defined as the least detector evidence a manipulation must reveal per unit of harm to the downstream task. The margin has a closed form, takes about $85\,μ$s per certificate, yields a minimum-evidence attack, and identifies task-relevant directions the detector cannot see. On a 17-channel industrial telemetry benchmark, a detector that flags 82.8\% of random single-channel corruptions is first-order blind on 64.7\% of task/subset pairs in an audit of one- to four-channel subsets. Task-conditioned manipulations cause more than twice as many falsely reassuring errors as generic stealthy ones, and more of them evade the alarm on four of five splits, mainly at small budgets. Used to prioritize audits on held-out subsets, the margin finds a median of four verified failures in ten checks, compared with none for random order and two for alarm-based ranking, and performs comparably to the task-gradient baseline. It also ranks vulnerable configurations of the learned GDN and TranAD detectors and of a five-source crop-yield panel.
items.title: Quantifying and Prioritizing Stealthy Source-Manipulation Threats Against Multi-Source Anomaly Detectors

items.summary: Deploying LLM agents in specialized domains often require fine-grained task-specific procedures and knowledge a general model lacks, yet parameter training is costly and non-interpretable, and hand-engineered agent systems shift the cost to expert labor. Episodic memory updates at context level, but single agent adaptation struggles to alleviate cross-task interference, especially with complex tasks such as multi-application navigation or data pool analysis. Although multi-agent evolution alleviates this problem, existing methods lack clear definitions on update rules and rely on the backbone model to decide where and how much the system changes. This ill-scoped evolution makes learning follow the backbone's structural preferences rather than the observed failures: one backbone accumulates skills while another spawns agents. We present EMMA (structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent workflow synthesis), which treats the configuration of a multi-agent system (controller routing memory, specialists inheriting a generalist prompt, and per-step procedural skills) as episodic memory. EMMA makes the ownership and admissibility of updates explicit: a reflector assigns each diagnosed failure to the scope owning its correction and proposes one edit within it, and backbone-independent guards keep every accepted edit scoped, incremental and bounded. Across KramaBench, AppWorld and BBEH with five backbones and four baselines (ACE, GEPA, EvoMAS and ADAS), EMMA attains the best overall performance on every benchmark, up to 32.5% over the strongest baseline, maintains consistent improvements across backbones, and uses 17-38% fewer training executions than the most efficient baseline.
items.title: EMMA: Structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent Workflow Synthesis

items.summary: Supervised pairwise graph representations convert pairwise predictive relations into sample-specific graphs, but graph-level accuracy does not by itself show that higher-order topology carries the signal. In a controlled Transformer error-detection task, supervised pairwise graphs outperform attention-as-adjacency (ROC-AUC $0.839$ versus $0.559$; the comparable no-confidence pair is $0.687$ versus $0.559$), but their apparent advantage over model confidence disappears after controlling for sequence length, which is almost perfectly recoverable from the pooled hidden state ($R^2=0.9995$). On published HCP Emotion ensemble graphs, signed node aggregation already acts as an ensemble of supervised pairwise predictions. Edge magnitude alone is near chance; topology-aware augmentations change ROC-AUC by at most $0.004$, with only sign-separated degree showing small positive changes across all tested graph sizes, while a validation-tuned three-layer GCN provides no measurable improvement over the signed node-summary baseline. A Fisher post-hoc corrector satisfies its distribution-agnostic guarantees across the evaluated feature representations and remains stable under reduced labelled budgets; in a near-error-free fMRI calibration regime the bound correctly becomes statistically uninformative. A separate cross-attention analysis identifies a redundant reversal circuit and downstream EOS-timing and copy failures. Higher-order topology should therefore be credited only after local supervised evidence and recoverable nuisance variables have been excluded.
items.title: Interpreting Supervised Pairwise Graph Representations: Local Evidence, Confounding, and Provable Post-hoc Correction

items.summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly deployed across sequences of related tasks, yet they often fail to retain and improve their knowledge over time. Existing approaches convert interaction trajectories into memories or reusable skills, but experience is not automatically reliable knowledge. Automatically collected skills and memories can propagate errors, mislead, and corrupt useful knowledge. To address this gap, we introduce Knowledge Evolution from Expertise and Lessons (KEEL), an agent-agnostic framework that uses verifier evidence to transform successful behavior into reusable skills and failures into corrective lessons. As new evidence accumulates, individual skill claims can be supported, contradicted, replaced, or retired. On SkillFlow benchmark, KEEL improves task success by 4.2 to 21.7 percentage points over the no-knowledge baseline, compared with gains of 2.4 to 9.6 points from SkillFlow's default method. Ablations show that skills and lessons are complementary. These results show that reliable continual agent learning depends not simply on accumulating experience, but on continually validating and evolving the knowledge derived from it. Our code is available at: https://github.com/microsoft/KEEL-TTCL26.
items.title: Holding a Steady Course: Knowledge Evolution from Expertise and Lessons for Continual Agent Learning

items.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks. Yet their memory and collaboration architectures often remain static, constraining continued adaptation and improvement over time. Recent work addresses this limitation by evolving memory or collaboration based on interaction experience. However, updates to these interdependent components are not necessarily aligned: an evolved workflow may require experience that memory does not provide, while evolved memory may encode guidance that the workflow cannot use. To address this problem, we propose CoEvolve, a skill-centered framework for aligned memory--collaboration evolution. CoEvolve represents reusable local collaboration patterns as skills that link evolving collaboration decisions to their supporting memories. It further compares original and counterfactual trajectories to identify local evolution signals, which coordinate updates to the skill library, skill memory, and executor memories across rounds. Experiments on the ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks confirm that CoEvolve achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated baselines, while ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of aligned co-evolution and counterfactual-guided evolution.
items.title: CoEvolve: Counterfactual-Guided Co-Evolution of Memory and Collaboration in Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but their understanding of physical dynamics remains limited. Video world models can capture scene dynamics, yet generating future videos introduces high latency into the control loop. We introduce PDRVLA, whose lightweight Physical Dynamics Module extracts physical tokens from vision--language features to condition action generation without online video generation. The module learns through direct prediction of future RGB, depth, and optical-flow features, with auxiliary supervision through a frozen pretrained video world model. Training relies entirely on publicly available data, expanded through human-to-robot synthesis, subtask annotation, and embodied chain-of-thought (ECoT) annotation. Across four simulation benchmarks, PDRVLA achieves success rates of 99.3% on LIBERO, 89.9% on LIBERO-Plus, 93.6% on RoboTwin~2.0, and 81.5% on SimplerEnv. Ablations show improved future prediction with world-model supervision and evaluate how subtask conditioning, future object-pose supervision, and ECoT training affect action success.
items.title: PDRVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model with Physical Dynamics Representations

items.summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) require both effective coordination and specialized task execution. Existing prompt optimization approaches typically couple these functions within agent-specific prompts. We introduce Coordinator-Executor Prompt Optimization (CEPO), a general framework for improving prompt optimization in MAS. CEPO separates system-level coordination from agent-level execution through a shared coordinator prompt and agent-specific executor prompts, and guides their updates according to their respective roles. This structure allows shared coordination rules to be refined consistently across agents while keeping execution instructions separately adjustable. CEPO provides the prompt structure and optimization guidance, while existing prompt optimizers perform the underlying search. Extensive experiments spanning 11 benchmarks across four domains demonstrate that applying CEPO to four existing prompt optimizers consistently improves their performance. Ablations and qualitative analyses support the proposed design, while controlled studies on a document-understanding MAS further demonstrate improved optimization budget efficiency and performance scaling with the number of agents.
items.title: CEPO: A General Framework for Improving Prompt Optimization in Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Scenario-Robust Coordinated Beamforming for Cell-Free ISAC under Imperfect CSI This repository contains the full simulator, notebooks, configuration files, and result checkpoints for the paper “Scenario-Robust Coordinated Beamforming for Cell-Free ISAC under Imperfect CSI: Outage Control and Sensing-Information Preservation.” The method, SR-CBSA, is a scenario-robust coordinated block successive convex approximation scheme for joint communication and sensing beamforming in distributed cell-free massive MIMO ISAC networks under pilot-based CSI uncertainty. It enforces direct global received-signal SINR constraints over sampled channel-error scenarios, preserves target-directed sensing power and a transmit-side azimuth-information surrogate, and stabilizes sequential per-access-point updates through trust regions, damping, proximal regularization, and penalized feasibility slack. Training, held-out validation, the physical true channel, and unseen-error test scenarios are kept strictly separate, so the reported gains reflect genuine robustness rather than overfitting to the sampled errors. The code reproduces every result in the paper from seed-controlled experiments: the paired Monte Carlo study across 5, 10, 15, and 20 dB pilot SNR, the same-realization method comparison, the QoS-target feasibility sweep, the responsibility-rule ablation, the scenario-count and synchronization-error sensitivity studies, the full-rank and locally low-rank scalability cases, and the baseline comparisons including the adapted JointOpt framework and a feasible max-min robust SOCP relaxation. All optimization uses CVXPY with CLARABEL, runs on CPU, and writes CSV checkpoints so long runs can be resumed and verified independently. Set the experiment flags in the configuration cell, run the notebook top to bottom, and the module and figures are regenerated automatically. See the README for environment setup, the flag-to-experiment mapping, and the fixed seeds used for each reported table and figure.
items.title: Scenario-Robust Coordinated Beamforming for Cell-Free ISAC under Imperfect CSI: Outage Control and Sensing-Information Preservation

items.summary: Edge-centric IoT systems are increasingly evaluated through sensor values or platform features, yet the telemetry pipeline itself, the sequence of sensing, serialization, message mediation, ingestion, and persistence, is rarely released as a measurable object. This limits reproducible benchmarking of timeliness, provenance, and operational cost, especially in early-stage IoT design where real deployments and high-quality open data are often unavailable. I present a measurement-first edge IoT testbed and dataset that elevate timeliness, provenance, and energy to first-class telemetry dimensions. The testbed operationalizes a role-based event-driven architecture with explicit Source-Broker-Aggregator responsibilities and a schema-governed TelemetryMessage envelope (Avro) that embeds correlation identifiers and a uniform, cross-role vocabulary of stage-level timestamps. To trace mediation effects, I extend an MQTT broker (Eclipse Mosquitto) with a plugin that annotates messages with high-precision ingress/egress timestamps. I release the dataset in a dual representation: (i) replayable raw events as compressed Avro streams and (ii) analysis-ready long-format Parquet tables partitioned for efficient query and benchmarking, generated by a deterministic raw-to-tabular transformation pipeline. The contribution is an integrated engineering artifact and dataset built from established components. The demonstration describes one deployment through latency summaries, measurement-context distributions, and energy aggregates; it does not establish a new attribution method or a controlled performance benchmark. By co-releasing heterogeneous telemetry with pipeline timing and energy signals in both replayable and queryable forms, the artifact provides a basis for reproducible exploratory analysis and subsequent benchmarking studies.
items.title: Making the Telemetry Pipeline Measurable: An Edge IoT Testbed and Dataset for End-to-End Latency, Provenance, and Energy-Aware Benchmarking

items.summary: Two follow-up papers built on this study's blind multi-model collection were accepted (poster) at NeurIPS 2026 workshops: Verification Theater: Measured Failure Modes of AI Verifier Panels (Who Verifies the Agents?) and Weakly Discriminative, Not Repaired by Profile Injection, and Manipulable: Self-Confidence in LLM Evaluation (TAE). Version of record: SSRN 7191261 , DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7191261 . Cite that version. The same text is also at https://vadymchernets.netlify.app/architectural-trust.html and https://github.com/vadimchernets/papers/tree/main/architectural-trust . Agentic commerce turns AI from an advisor into a transacting party, collapsing search, comparison, cart, and payment into a single delegated act and removing the review points where humans once caught errors. It arrives at an awkward moment: sixty percent of UK consumers surveyed say they would abandon an AI shopping agent after a single mistake, and most would trust no organization at all to run one on their behalf. This paper introduces architectural trust. As consumers delegate consequential decisions to AI agents, I argue, warranted trust migrates from the properties of the AI model to the verifiable architecture of the service above it. The constructs already available attach trust to organizations, to a single automated system, or to algorithmic advice, and none of them makes the decision-producing process verifiable by the truster under autonomous delegation. Architectural trust fills that gap with three checkable properties: diversity (independent models whose agreement calibrates confidence and whose divergence is surfaced), evidence (tamper-evident, replayable decision records), and neutrality (auditable independence from any vendor, merchant, or outcome). The mechanism was measured on the machine side first. Across a pre-registered sixteen-model benchmark and an August 2026 flagship-tier wave spanning eleven frontier laboratories, cross-model agreement priced correctness where a model's own confidence could not. Answers reproduced by another, blindly queried model were 1.9–3.2 times as likely to be correct. On a frozen SimpleQA subsample (Wei et al., 2024), 46.6% of the flagship answers offered at stated confidence ≥ 80 were wrong (a rate specific to this roster, not a universal constant), while a fixed three-model disagreement gate removed 82.1% of those confident failures (95% CI 79.9–84.1) at 30.5% coverage. In a post hoc analysis of the August 2026 snapshot, two flagships answering blindly (gpt-5.6-sol and claude-fable-5) agreed on 69.6% of the 1,459 pooled questions, and their agreed answer was correct 98.1% of the time, against 95.3% for the stronger one alone on the same pool. The signal reproduces on 267 Wikidata-verified commerce product facts. A larger reasoning budget bought 3.1 points of stated confidence and no measurable accuracy: more compute buys confidence, not correctness. A unanimously confident panel can still be wrong, and there agreement certifies the shared error. I then carry the mechanism into behavior in a pre-registered, incentive-compatible consumer experiment (US and UK; 119 valid participants in the primary cohort, 133 with a soft-launch cohort pooled; 200 planned). Where a consumer would otherwise accept a confident wrong recommendation, the disagreement display cut acceptance sharply, from 74% to 24% on the qualifying item (pooled cohort). A powered, stimulus-sampled replication is planned. On the one item of unanimous confident consensus (pooled n = 133) the display raised acceptance of the shared error from 87% to 95%, which reproduces the mechanism's boundary in human behavior. items.summary: Memory-agent benchmarks often collapse retrieval and answer generation into one score, making it hard to tell whether a failure comes from missing an update or from not using an update that was already retrieved. We examine this distinction on the single-hop FactConsolidation task of MemoryAgentBench. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 6K-history BM25 accuracy drops from 45% to 32% when the retrieved evidence budget grows from 64 to 512 tokens, even though a gold-assisted post-hoc audit finds the newest statement in every retrieved set. Most of the errors occur on questions that also contain an obsolete statement version. Under a frozen prompt and equal four-statement evidence size, replacing one unrelated statement with the obsolete competing statement reduces accuracy from 100% to 44.6% for Qwen2.5 and from 100% to 87.8% for Qwen3-14B, with all 50 harmful paired flips classified as stale. A 32K-history replication likewise favors BM25-64 over BM25-512 (69% versus 58%). These results suggest that retrieving the correct fact is not enough. An obsolete competing statement can be more harmful than an unrelated piece of evidence of the same size.
items.title: When Retrieval Is Not Enough: Obsolete Facts in Agent Memory

items.summary: TEMPLATE-DIRECTED MASS FABRICATION OF BIOMEDICAL MICRO/NANOROBOTS AT THE LIMIT is a 770-page, high-density English research monograph on scaling template replication without losing dimensional fidelity, surface integrity, functional consistency or scientific traceability. The book treats the template as a stateful manufacturing ancestor rather than a passive tool. Every cavity and replication cycle is registered so that template wear, release-coating decay, demolding force, replica bias, particle residue, spatial defect clustering and functional outcomes can be linked across the full template life. Its central falsifiable claim asks whether lifetime-aware monitoring can predict rising defect probability before damage spreads. Thirty mathematically distinct research plates cover cavity filling, squeeze flow, material relaxation, cure conversion, shrinkage, residual stress, adhesion, demolding, fracture, Archard wear, coating survival, hidden wear states, geometry transfer, Hausdorff error, spatial point processes, defect ancestry, survival hazards, change points, capability, conservative yield, hierarchical variance and qualified-part cost. Across 82 chapters and 410 single-page studies, the monograph develops replication physics, release mechanics, template wear, spatial defect genealogy, adaptive process control, functional qualification, lifecycle economics and independent transfer. Two hundred Research Gates define blind challenges, strong comparators, evidence packages, hard stops and successor forks. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos present genuinely different witnesses, challenge artifacts, estimators, controllers, economic falsifiers, release keys and handoff kits. The work is explicitly nonclinical and hypothesis-generating. It does not claim a completed manufacturing campaign, human treatment, autonomous in-body efficacy or regulatory approval. Its release rule is conjunctive: wear, demolding force, geometry, defect clustering, unselected yield, task function and traceability must pass together over the complete template life. items.summary: Training large language models (LLMs) in sub-8-bit arithmetic promises substantial gains in memory bandwidth and compute throughput, yet FP4 formats introduce quantization error severe enough to destabilize optimization if left unaddressed. We present ALTO, an open-source training recipe for GPT-OSS-20B, a 20-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, on the MLPerf Small MoE Training benchmark under the MXFP4 microscaling format. The recipe combines established techniques from Abecassis, Felix et al. [arXiv:2509.25149] (hybrid 1D/2D block quantization, randomized Hadamard transforms, and stochastic rounding) with a simplified weight de-oscillation scheme adapted from TetraJet-v2 [arXiv:2510.27527]. On C4 validation at global batch size 16, MXFP4 + RHT + SR + de-oscillation reaches a validation loss of 3.3350 at 16,128 steps, only 0.007 above the BF16 baseline (3.3283), closing roughly 50% of the gap left by MXFP4 without de-oscillation (3.3418). Measured by steps to reach the MLPerf quality target (validation loss 3.34), de-oscillation cuts the FP4 convergence overhead relative to BF16 from +20.0% to +5.0%. We also report negative end-to-end results from differential gradient estimation, outlier clipping, and macro-block scaling, despite each showing operator-level SNR gains. All experiments use simulated MXFP4 kernels on AMD MI300 hardware and wall-clock speed has not been optimized.
items.title: Training an MoE LLM in MXFP4: How We Closed the Gap to BF16

items.summary: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma
items.title: SOMA: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Egocentric Behavior and Body-Motion Understanding
